title: Tempos, difficult keys and playing on the changes
summary: Goodwin describes jam-session key tests and horn players becoming chord-conscious in the mid-thirties; Lovett has noticed no tempo change.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Right. This is a long one -- question but I'll read it. How have tempos changed over the years? When did certain more difficult keys become widely used? When did you first understand the concept of playing on changes?
Well, as a drummer, Baby and I are both drummers, Crook, we probably don't have that much of a problem. Would you want to say anything to that, Baby?
We're out of that. Crook is in it.
Crook, did you want to say anything about this?

Well, I've got to answer that this way. Again I would like to go back to the '30s, the early '30s is when I first recognized that musicians -- well I might call them horn blowers and that would take in saxophone and brass and they would -- we would be having a jam session and we would -- well possibly some person would come along that didn't think -- we didn't think he could blow so well and we would immediately speak about -- well these are musicians that understood their instruments pretty well and they could improvise pretty well and also could read pretty well -- so they would, you know, you didn't want this particular guy on the stand and the piano player would look over and say, "Okay fellows, let's take a trip through the keys".

Now this means you would start at a high key and then possibly go down or vice-versa. Now each one of these keys would be a half step. See if he started on A-flat, you'd go to A natural and then B-flat, you know, and B natural and you would play this particular song in each one of those keys.
Well, if you wasn't adept on the instrument, well you couldn't cut it, so you'd have to leave, and I think though during the '30s when the -- in the middle '30s I'll say, it
began to change and it began to become each horn blower become more chord conscious because it gives him a wider range to play and to begin to listen to play.
Right, and then he began to listen to things that he had never played before and I think this is where your change came.
Thanks Crook. You know Baby, it does say something about tempo here. Have you noticed over the years many tempo changes? Well, go ahead, you say it.
No, I haven't noticed them. The same thing all the time, especially for drummers.
I would have thought so. You're either playing fast, slow or medium or something in between and I guess it's always been that way in the field of jazz.
